P3
Let G be a directed graph. Define the transitive closure GT as the directed graph sharing
P4
the same vertex set as G, where an edge u →v exists in GT if and only if there is a
P5
directed path from u to v in G. Furthermore, define a transitive reduction of G to be a
P6
graph with the minimum number of edges such that its transitive closure is identical to
P7
GT. Given that a graph may generally admit multiple transitive reductions, prove that
P8
G possesses a unique transitive reduction if and only if G is acyclic.
P9
Solution:
**Solution:**
*Proof of “if” (acyclic implies unique):* Suppose G is a directed acyclic graph (DAG).
Then the reachability relation in GT is a **partial order** on the vertices (no cycles means
no pair of distinct vertices reach each other in both directions). In a partial order, an edge
u →v is **essential** (cannot be removed) if and only if u is *covered* by v – that is, u < v
in the reachability order and there is no intermediate vertex w with u < w < v . These
*covering edges* form a minimal set that generates all reachability via transitivity, and this
set is unique. In fact, any transitive reduction of G must contain *exactly* those covering
edges: if u →v is a cover in GT, no alternate path u →· · · →v exists, so any subgraph
preserving reachability must include u →v. Conversely, if an edge u →v is *not* a cover
(meaning u →· · · →v via some intermediate w exists), then u →v is redundant and would
be omitted in a minimal transitive reduction. It follows that the **transitive reduction of a
DAG G is unique**: it consists exactly of the covering relations (edges that have no shorter
indirect route) . This is the familiar *Hasse diagram* of the partial order, which is uniquely
determined by GT.
*Proof of “only if” (unique implies acyclic):* Now assume G is *not* acyclic, i.e. G
contains at least one directed cycle. We will show that in this case G admits **multiple
distinct** transitive reductions, so it cannot have a unique one .
Let S be a strongly
connected component of G that contains a cycle and let |S| = m ≥2. In GT, every pair of
distinct vertices in S is mutually reachable. Any transitive reduction must therefore include
at least m edges within S, because a directed graph on m vertices needs at least m edges to
remain strongly connected (for example, a cycle through all m vertices). We construct two
different edge-minimal subgraphs of S that both preserve full reachability:
- **Cycle 1 (clockwise):** list the vertices of S as v1, v2, . . . , vm in some order and include
the m edges
This directed cycle uses m edges and clearly makes every vi reachable from every other vj
by traversing around the cycle.
- **Cycle 2 (counterclockwise):** include instead the m edges
This is a directed cycle through the same vertices in the opposite order, again with m edges
and again strongly connecting all vertices.
Because S is strongly connected in G, each edge used in Cycle 2 corresponds to a pair
of vertices that were already reachable in the original graph (indeed, GT contains *every*
directed pair among vertices in S). Thus *both* Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 are valid transitive
reductions of G: each has the minimum m edges and their reachability (transitive closures) is
the same as GT on S. Moreover, Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 differ by at least one edge – for instance,
Cycle 1 contains v1 →v2 whereas Cycle 2 contains v2 →v1, so they are not identical sets of
edges. We have exhibited two distinct transitive reductions of G, so the transitive reduction
is **not unique**.
In summary, a directed graph G has a unique transitive reduction **if and only if**
G is acyclic. In the acyclic case, the reachability relation is a partial order with a unique
covering relation (unique minimal edge set) . In the presence of any directed cycle, multiple
different minimal edge-subsets can realize the same reachability, destroying uniqueness .
(This completes the proof.)
